The ICE BofA US High Yield OAS tracks the extra yield investors require to hold below-investment-grade bonds over comparable Treasuries. It is a widely-followed risk indicator in fixed income, often rising in periods of economic uncertainty, market turbulence, or rising default risk. The biweekly closing value helps forecasters track the evolving risk appetite and credit conditions in the U.S. market.

The OAS represents the average yield spread (in basis points) over Treasuries for U.S. high-yield (junk) bonds, adjusted for embedded options. This metric is widely watched as a gauge of credit market risk and sentiment.

numeric.title: How much will Nvidia's stock price returns exceed Microsoft's in these biweekly periods of Q2 2026? (Jun 15 - Jun 26)
numeric.resolution_criteria:
This question is a subquestion of a group question. This subquestion specifically pertains to (and resolves according to) the option 'Jun 15 - Jun 26'. The resolution criteria for the parent question is below. 

Each subquestion will resolve as the difference between the percent stock price return of [NVDA](https://finance.yahoo.com/quote/NVDA/history/) and that of [MSFT](https://finance.yahoo.com/quote/MSFT/history/) for the corresponding biweekly period, according to Yahoo Finance data.

Specifically, each subquestion will resolve as NVDA\_return - MSFT\_return.

Returns will be calculated as follows: If P₀ is the Adj Close price of a company stock on the last trading day or half-day *before* the start of the period and P₁ is the Adj Close price of the stock on the last trading day *of* the designated period, the percentage return will be calculated as:

$$
 \text{return} = 100 \times \frac{P1 - P0}{P0}
$$
numeric.fine_print:
* If Microsoft outperforms Nvidia, the corresponding subquestion will resolve as a negative number.
* If Yahoo Finance delays or ceases reporting these data or if it reports them in error, Metaculus might use alternative credible sources to resolve this question.
* Resolutions are based on the prices at the market close on the last trading day of the designated period. Further adjustments to Adj Close prices after that will not cause subquestions to re-resolve.

***

For example, for the period Jun 9, 2025 - Jun 20, 2025, the subquestion would resolve based on the following calculations:

NVDA\_P₀ \= 141.71 (the Adj Close price on Jun 6)

NVDA\_P₁ \= 143.85 (the Close price on Jun 20)

NVDA\_return \= 100 × (143.85 - 141.71) / 141.71 \= 1.510

MSFT\_P₀ \= 470.38 (the Adj Close price on Jun 6)

MSFT\_P₁ \= 477.40 (the Close price on Jun 20)

MSFT\_return \= 100 × (477.40 - 470.38) / 470.38 \= 1.4924

And the resolution would be 1.510 - 1.494 \= **0.016** percentage points (pp).

***

Historical values for the VIX are available from TradingView [here](https://www.tradingview.com/symbols/CBOE-VIX/).

numeric.title: How many journalists in the US will face criminal charges related to their work before 2027?
numeric.resolution_criteria: This question resolves as the number of incidents of journalists arrested and/or charged with crimes in the United States in 2025 and 2026 according to the [U.S. Press Freedom Tracker](https://pressfreedomtracker.us/arrest-criminal-charge/?).
numeric.fine_print:
If the resolution source is no longer available or fails to be maintained, Metaculus may name an alternative resolution source, may use [credible sources](https://www.metaculus.com/faq/#definitions) to resolve the question, or may **annul** the question. Alternative sources should follow similar methodology as the one outlined by the [U.S. Press Freedom Tracker](https://pressfreedomtracker.us/frequently-asked-questions/):

> The U.S. Press Freedom Tracker adopts a functional definition of who is a journalist. It doesn’t matter whether the individual has a press pass or went to journalism school, whether they work for The New York Times or work for themselves. What matters is whether the person was performing an act of journalism. The Tracker will count journalists whose rights to gather and disseminate information were violated in the course of their work or as a result of their work.
numeric.description: While the United States has strong constitutional protections for freedom of the press, the use of federal criminal charges has occurred, albeit rarely, in its history. When such prosecutions occur, they typically involve allegations related to national security, unauthorized possession or dissemination of classified information, or obstruction of justice. In some instances, journalists have faced legal exposure for refusing to reveal sources, trespassing during newsgathering, or alleged violations of computer or wiretapping laws. In his second term, President Trump has been critical of the press and has[<u> previously called for the jailing of journalists who publish leaked materials</u>](https://thehill.com/homenews/3820172-trump-calls-for-jailing-journalists-who-broke-supreme-courts-draft-abortion-decision/).

numeric.title: What will be the maximum close value of the volatility index (VIX) for the latter half of 2025 and 2026?
numeric.resolution_criteria: This question resolves as the maximum close value of the [Cboe Volatility Index](https://www.cboe.com/tradable_products/vix/) (VIX) after June 30, 2025 and before January 1, 2027, using as the official resolution source the [downloadable CSV file](https://www.cboe.com/tradable_products/vix/vix_historical_data/) provided by Cboe.
numeric.fine_print:
* If the official resolution source is unavailable, Metaculus may use another source that presents the same data. 
* This question will resolve as the maximum CLOSE value listed in the resolution CSV.
numeric.description:
According to [S\&P Global:](https://www.spglobal.com/spdji/en/vix-intro/)

> The Cboe Volatility Index, better known as VIX, projects the probable range of movement in the U.S. equity markets, above and below their current level, in the immediate future. Specifically, VIX measures the implied volatility of the S\&P 500® (SPX) for the next 30 days. When implied volatility is high, the VIX level is high and the range of likely values is broad. When implied volatility is low, the VIX level is low and the range is narrow.

> Since VIX reaches its highest levels when the stock market is most unsettled, the media tend to refer to VIX as a fear gauge. In the sense that VIX is a measure of sentiment—of worry in particular—the description is on the mark.

In the past few years, the VIX has had the following history:

<iframe src="https://fred.stlouisfed.org/graph/graph-landing.php?g=1FAjQ&width=585&height=500" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" style="overflow:hidden; width:585px; height:525px;" loading="lazy"></iframe>  
The historical average level of the VIX, since its beginnings in 1990, [has been](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1T256TzUPpHLUJuygskfRqiLCitBJKI3hkwilQaDGyBk/edit?gid=1873463336#gid=1873463336) 19.5. During March 2020, when COVID-19 began rapidly spreading in the United States, the VIX's maximum reached 85.5, with an average daily high of 65. During the Global Financial Crisis of 2008, the VIX's maximum was 89.5, reached on October 24, 2008, corresponding with [Bloody Friday](https://www.thenational.scot/news/17002469.bloody-friday-financial-crash-went-10-years-ago-today/), when markets worldwide crashed up to 10% on that single day.  During the month of the September 11th 2001 terrorist attack on the World Trade Center and Pentagon, the VIX maxed at 49.

During the entire administration of Joe Biden, the VIX's daily high averaged 20.6, with the maximum being 65.7, reached on August 5, 2024, when the VIX had its [biggest ever one-day spike](https://www.bis.org/publ/bisbull95.pdf), when the US markets opened after the Japanese stock market was down 12% in one day. On the final full trading day before Trump's inauguration, the VIX was 16.0. At the time of this question, in the first two months of Donald Trump's administration, the VIX's daily high has averaged 20.1, with the maximum hitting 29.57 on March 11, 2025, amid talk of Trump [threatening to hike tariffs](https://fortune.com/2025/03/11/trumps-tariff-threats-caused-vix-surge-is-it-momentary-spike-start-of-a-global-contagion/).

numeric.title: What will Donald Trump's net approval be on November 2, 2026?
numeric.resolution_criteria: This question will resolve as Donald Trump's net approval rating, defined as approval minus disapproval, on November 2, 2026, according to data from the [Silver Bulletin](https://www.natesilver.net/p/trump-approval-ratings-nate-silver-bulletin).
numeric.fine_print:
* A positive value corresponds to a higher approval than disapproval rating. A negative value corresponds to a lower approval than disapproval rating.
* This question will resolve as the November 2, 2026 value when accessed by Metaculus on or after November 9, 2026. Later revisions to the data are immaterial. If no value for November 2, 2026 is available when accessed by Metaculus, the closest values will be used to resolve this question, provided that these are for any date after October 26, 2026 and before November 9, 2026. In that case, the resolution will be calculated as follows: If there is one, unambiguous closest value (e.g., a value for November 4 is shown on the site but not one for October 31), the question will resolve using that. If there are two equidistant closest values, then the question will resolve using their average.
numeric.description:
Presidents tend to go through a "[honeymoon period](https://politicaldictionary.com/words/honeymoon-period/)" shortly after they are elected, where they enjoy high public approval ratings. Though presidents like Eisenhower and Kennedy enjoyed honeymoon periods lasting a year or more, these periods have [grown shorter](https://news.gallup.com/poll/121391/obama-honeymoon-continues-months-recent-average.aspx) in recent decades, potentially due to increased polarization and the rapid news cycle, with modern presidents often seeing their initial support wane within months.

In his first presidential term, Donald Trump had a positive approval rating [only for the first two weeks in office](https://projects.fivethirtyeight.com/trump-approval-ratings/), according to 538, with his approval rating averaging slightly higher than 40% throughout his term and his disapproval a little over 50%. The 2024 election was more successful for Trump something that was reflected in [his approval ratings](https://www.natesilver.net/p/trump-approval-ratings-nate-silver-bulletin) for the first two months in office. However, his net approval rating (approval minus disapproval rating) as of mid April has been consistently dropping since the inauguration, at an average rate of 0.2 percentage points per day, according to data from the [Silver Bulletin](https://www.natesilver.net/p/trump-approval-ratings-nate-silver-bulletin).

numeric.title: How many people will work for the US federal government in November 2026?
numeric.resolution_criteria: This question will resolve as the number of federal employees in November 2026, in thousands, according to data presented for [All Employees, Federal](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/CES9091000001) by the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (FRED).
numeric.description:
When Donald Trump was inaugurated as the 47th President of the United States in January 2025, his Administration quickly made plans for widespread reductions in the 3 million-strong federal labor force, [which was described](https://www.npr.org/2025/03/06/nx-s1-5310542/federal-workforce-other-countries-compared) as having "brought turmoil to a sector long seen as a bastion of stability." On a human level, this has been reported to have a high personal cost to the federal workers affected, with a suicide prevention manager at the Department of Veterans Affairs [saying](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/doge/federal-workers-gripped-mental-health-instability-trump-cuts-rcna194485), "When you have a purpose in life and you found your thing, and then all of a sudden it’s being destroyed — you lose all hope."

[According to President Trump](https://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/documents/remarks-prior-cabinet-meeting-15) before a cabinet meeting, in response to some of the criticism:

> We're cutting down government. We're cutting down the size of government. We have to. We're bloated. We're sloppy. We have a lot of people that aren't doing their job. We have a lot of people that don't exist.

Some recent examples of announced mass layoffs (officially called [Reductions in Force](https://www.opm.gov/policy-data-oversight/workforce-restructuring/reductions-in-force-rif/) or RIF) have been:

* Eighty-two thousand employees of the Veterans Administration planned to be cut, out of about 482,000. ([Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/world/us/department-veterans-affairs-cut-80000-jobs-part-trump-cuts-2025-03-05/))
* Terminating almost half the Department of Education, going from 4,133 workers to 2,183. ([CBS News](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/department-of-education-job-cuts/) ([The Hill](https://thehill.com/homenews/education/5190161-linda-mcmahon-education-department-mass-layoffs/))
* Up to 65% of the Environmental Protection Agency's workforce, 11,000 workers, terminated as part of plan to have "maximum elimination" of job functions not specifically required to law. ([Fed News](https://www.govexec.com/workforce/2025/02/agencies-deliver-large-scale-rif-plans-two-weeks/403303/))
* About 2,000 cut at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration since the start of January, almost 20% of the pre-Trump numbers ([CBS News](https://abcnews.go.com/Politics/noaa-braces-mass-layoffs-fueling-concerns-lifesaving-weather/story?id=119730398)), including [National Weather Service](https://thebeaconnews.org/stories/2025/03/17/national-weather-service-job-cuts-layoffs-noaa-nws/) and [National Hurricane Center](https://www.poynter.org/reporting-editing/2025/noaa-cuts-doge-elon-musk-meteorologists/) staffers.

For more information see the [RIF watch](https://www.govexec.com/workforce/2025/02/rif-watch-see-which-agencies-are-laying-federal-workers/403342/) tracking page maintained by the Government Executive publication, which reports that the Office of Management and Budget and the Office of Personnel Management has plans for the "maximum elimination" of roles not required by law, which amounts to about 700,000 employees.

Historically, the numbers of federal government employees has been as follows:

<iframe loading="lazy" style="overflow:hidden; width:100%; height:550px;" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" src="https://fred.stlouisfed.org/graph/graph-landing.php?g=1HWn9&width=100%25&height=475"></iframe>

numeric.title: How much crude oil will the US produce monthly in the second quarter of 2026?
numeric.resolution_criteria: This question will resolve as the average monthly crude oil production during the months of April, May, and June, 2026, according to [data published by the US Energy Information Administration](https://www.eia.gov/dnav/pet/hist/LeafHandler.ashx?n=PET\&s=MCRFPUS1\&f=M) (EIA). The question will resolve by taking the sum of US field production of crude oil over the three months in question and dividing the sum by three to arrive at the average monthly production.
numeric.fine_print:
* Please note that as of April 2025 the source provides the data in "thousand barrels", and this question uses the same units.
* The question resolves when data for each respective month through June 2026 is first available. Later updates or revisions to the data after the question has resolved are immaterial.
numeric.description:
President Donald Trump has made expanding oil and gas production a [key issue](https://thehill.com/policy/energy-environment/4984398-trump-incoming-administration-oil-gas-mining-energy-permitting/) during his campaign, and on the first day of his second term [declared a national energy emergency](https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/01/declaring-a-national-energy-emergency/). The emergency declaration ordered, among other things:

> The heads of executive departments and agencies (“agencies”) shall identify and exercise any lawful emergency authorities available to them, as well as all other lawful authorities they may possess, to facilitate the identification, leasing, siting, production, transportation, refining, and generation of domestic energy resources, including, but not limited to, on Federal lands.

In a subsequent [address](https://www.whitehouse.gov/remarks/2025/03/remarks-by-president-trump-in-joint-address-to-congress/) to Congress Trump [said](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-sDtdCzMIKA):

> As you’ve heard me say many times, we have more liquid gold under our feet than any nation on Earth and by far.  And now I’ve fully authorized the most talented team ever assembled to go and get it.  It’s called drill, baby, drill.

The US Energy Information Administration tracks [monthly US field production of crude oil data on its website](https://www.eia.gov/dnav/pet/hist/LeafHandler.ashx?n=pet\&s=mcrfpus1\&f=m). According to the EIA, crude oil field production is [defined](https://www.eia.gov/tools/glossary/?id=petroleum) as follows:

> Represents crude oil production on leases, including [lease condensate](https://www.eia.gov/tools/glossary/index.php?id=L#lease_cond). Excludes [plant condensate](https://www.eia.gov/tools/glossary/index.php?id=P#plant_cond) and other processed liquids. **Note: In some EIA publications, field production includes NGPL production, in accordance with definitions used prior to January 2014.**

For crude oil production measurement:

> The volume of crude oil produced from oil reservoirs during given periods of time. The amount of such production for a given period is measured as volumes delivered from lease storage tanks (i.e., the point of custody transfer) to pipelines, trucks, or other media for transport to refineries or terminals with adjustments for (1) net differences between opening and closing lease inventories, and (2) basic sediment and water (BSw).

numeric.fine_print:
This question will resolve based upon the first release of the data for Q4 2026. Further revisions after this question has been resolved will not be considered.

When viewing the resolution source, please ensure (via the Edit Graph button) that:

* the denominator, *Current payments to the rest of the world: Imports of goods, Billions of Dollars, Seasonally Adjusted Annual Rate*, is set to Units of **Billions of Dollars**.

* *Modify frequency* is set to Quarterly.
numeric.description:
Since taking office for his second term on January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump has imposed some tariffs and threatened others. According to the Tax Foundation in [Trump Tariffs: Tracking the Economic Impact of the Trump Trade War](https://taxfoundation.org/research/all/federal/trump-tariffs-trade-war/), the following tariff policies have been announced:

<iframe src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/3Wq1f/4/" scrolling="yes" frameborder="0" style="overflow:hidden; width:670px; height:525px;" allowTransparency="true" loading="lazy" />  
According to the Tax Foundation, tariff increases could have significant effects when it comes to US economic output and government revenues, particularly if there retaliatory tariffs imposed by other countries. The Foundation further states:

> We estimate the average tariff rate on all imports will rise from 2.5 percent in 2024 to 8.4 percent, the highest average rate since 1946.

Since 1960, effective tariff rates in the US have been as follows:

<iframe src="https://fred.stlouisfed.org/graph/graph-landing.php?g=1FFWn&width=670&height=475" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" style="overflow:hidden; width:670px; height:525px;" allowTransparency="true" loading="lazy" />  
Other professional forecasters have projected similar large increases. For example, according to [Yale University's Budget Lab](https://budgetlab.yale.edu/research/fiscal-economic-and-distributional-effects-20-tariffs-china-and-25-tariffs-canada-and-mexico#:~:text=Fiscal%20impact%20The%20tariffs%20are%20the%20equivalent,would%20raise%20\$1.4%2D1.5%20trillion%20over%202026%2D35%20conventionally%2Dscored.), the total effects of just the 25% tariffs on Canada and Mexico, along with the 10% tariffs on China in addition to the 10% already imposed, could be enough to raise the effective tariff rate by 7 percentage points, up to approximately 10%. However, there have also been [speculations from investors](\(https://forbesswitzerland.com/trumps-tariff-bluster-fails-to-rattle-markets-as-investors-bet-on-short-lived-threats/\)) and [others](https://www.everythingsupplychain.com/are-trumps-tariffs-a-negotiation-strategy/) that Trump might be using threats as part of the process of dealmaking and that tariffs may not increase as much as expected.

numeric.title: What will be the Economist Democracy Index for the United States for 2026?
numeric.resolution_criteria: This question will resolve as the score of the United States in the 2026 report of the Democracy Index by the Economist Intelligence Unit.
numeric.fine_print: If the report has not been released before April 1, 2027, this question will not be scored as part of the POTUS Predictions tournament.
numeric.description:
The Democracy Index is an index compiled by the [Economist Intelligence Unit](https://www.eiu.com/n/campaigns/democracy-index-2022/) that aims to measure the state of democracy in 167 countries (166 sovereign states, 164 UN members). It aggregates scores over 60 questions that are answered by either experts or public surveys and that belong into five categories:

* electoral process and pluralism (12 questions)
* functioning of government (14 questions)
* political participation (9 questions)
* political culture (8 questions)
* civil liberties (17 questions)

The index ranges from 0 to 10, with countries being classified into four types: authoritarian regimes (0 - 3.99), hybrid regimes (4 - 5.99), flawed democracies (6 - 7.99), and full democracies (8 - 10).

Since 2006, the US has seen a slight reduction in its scores, reaching 7.83 in 2024.

<iframe style="width: 95%; height: 500px;" loading="lazy" src="https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/democracy-index-eiu?tab=chart&country=~USA"></iframe>

numeric.title: What percent of US GDP will come from manufacturing in the first half of 2028?
numeric.resolution_criteria: This question will resolve as the average manufacturing share of GDP for Q1 and Q2, 2028, reported in the FRED series [Value Added by Industry: Manufacturing as a Percentage of GDP](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/VAPGDPMA) (VAPGDPMA).
numeric.fine_print: This question will resolve after both values have been published by FRED and when they are first accessed by Metaculus. Later revisions will not impact resolution.
numeric.description:
One of the most fundamental patterns in economic development is the progression from agriculture and resource extraction to industry to services. In this [three-stage model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three-sector_model), countries typically begin relying on primary activities, such as agriculture, mining, forestry, and fishing, then transition toward manufacturing and industrial production as productivity gains free up labor. In the final stage, mature economies pivot toward services. In the original model by Fisher, Clark, and Fourastié, these services were thought of as the transport, distribution and sale of goods, but later reconceptualisations of the model expanded the definition to include finance, healthcare, education, and entertainment.

This trend has become a particular concern for some US policymakers, with the GDP share of manufacturing dropping by more than a third from 1997 (16.1%) to 2021 (10.5%). At the same time the GDP share of manufacturing in the world dropped by less than 15 percent (from 19.0% to 16.5%).

<iframe src="https://data.worldbank.org/share/widget?indicators=NV.IND.MANF.ZS&locations=US-1W" width="600" height="450" frameborder="0" scrolling="no"></iframe>  
Declining manufacturing will likely have a negative impact on the US economy with [13 million workers](https://www.nist.gov/blogs/manufacturing-innovation-blog/manufacturing-america-contributing-our-economy-employment-and) employed in manufacturing jobs, and a large part of research and innovation being spearheaded by manufacturing companies. Indeed, some states would be [disproportionately affected](https://www.epi.org/publication/the-manufacturing-footprint-and-the-importance-of-u-s-manufacturing-jobs/#epi-toc-9) by manufacturing losses. Weak manufacturing would also lead to greater reliance on other countries and is thus often viewed as a [national security issue](https://www.cnas.org/publications/commentary/its-time-for-a-true-industrial-strategy-for-american-national-security); although [not everyone agrees](https://www.cato.org/publications/policy-analysis/manufactured-crisis-deindustrialization-free-markets-national-security#).

For these reasons, Trump [pledged](https://www.nytimes.com/2024/09/24/us/politics/trump-economic-policy.html) during his campaign that he would implement policies to increase the manufacturing capacity of the US. These included the early 2025 tariffs, but also other actions, such as the [removal of regulatory barriers](https://www.whitehouse.gov/fact-sheets/2025/05/fact-sheet-president-donald-j-trump-announces-actions-to-reduce-regulatory-barriers-to-domestic-pharmaceutical-manufacturing/) and [trade agrements with other nations](https://www.whitehouse.gov/fact-sheets/2025/05/fact-sheet-president-donald-j-trump-secures-historic-1-2-trillion-economic-commitment-in-qatar/). However, [many](https://edition.cnn.com/2025/04/10/business/manufacturing-us-jobs-trump-tariffs) [are skeptical](https://www.wsj.com/economy/jobs/will-anyone-take-the-factory-jobs-trump-wants-to-bring-back-to-america-f6cd377b) [that](https://www.npr.org/2025/05/09/nx-s1-5375146/trump-tariffs-factory-jobs-nostalgia) such policies will strengthen the US's manufacturing sector.

numeric.title: What will net outlays by the US government be in millions of dollars in FY 2028?
numeric.resolution_criteria: This question resolves as the amount of [Federal Net Outlays](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/FYONET) in the United States in millions of dollars in Fiscal Year 2028, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (FRED).
numeric.fine_print:
This question will resolve as the number shown by FRED, which represents millions of USD. For example, in 2024, this question would have resolved as **6,751,552**, as the net outlays were \$6,751,552,000,000. Therefore, when viewing the resolution source, please ensure (via the Edit Graph button) that:

* *Units* are set to **Millions of Dollars**.
* *Frequency* is set to Annual, Fiscal Year.

This question resolves based upon the first update by FRED incorporating federal net outlays for FY 2028. Further revisions after this question has been resolved will not be considered.
numeric.description:
Net outlays are the actual cash paid out by the US federal government in a given year, the equivalent of cash accounting. The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) [defines](https://budgetcounsel.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/10/page-77-78.pdf) outlays as: 

> The issuance of checks, disbursement of cash, or electronic transfer of funds made to liquidate a federal obligation. Outlays also occur when interest on the Treasury debt held by the public accrues and when the government issues bonds, notes, debentures, monetary credits, or other cash-equivalent instruments in order to liquidate obligations. Also, under credit reform, the credit subsidy cost is recorded as an outlay when a direct or guaranteed loan is disbursed. An outlay is not recorded for repayment of debt principal, disbursements to the public by federal credit programs for direct loan obligations and loan guarantee commitments made in fiscal year 1992 or later, disbursements from deposit funds, and refunds of receipts that result from overpayments. Outlays during a fiscal year may be for payment of obligations incurred in prior years (prior-year obligations) or in the same year. Outlays, therefore, flow in part from unexpended balances of prior-year budgetary resources and in part from budgetary resources provided for the year in which the money is spent.

In 2024, federal government outlays were \$6.75 trillion and made up 23% of the US's Gross Domestic Product (GDP). On January 20, 2025, Donald J. Trump was inaugurated as the 47th US President, and that same day he [established](https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/01/establishing-and-implementing-the-presidents-department-of-government-efficiency/) the Department of Governmental Efficiencey (DOGE), headed by Elon Musk. Musk has [stated a goal](https://www.yahoo.com/news/elon-musk-and-doge-promised-up-to-2-trillion-in-government-savings-how-much-have-they-actually-saved-so-far-201718142.html) of saving up to \$2 trillion annual expenditures by 2026. At the time of this question, the [DOGE website](https://doge.gov/savings) has tallied \$130 billion in savings.

In FY 2024, federal budget allocations [were](https://www.visualcapitalist.com/breaking-down-the-u-s-governments-2024-fiscal-year/) as follows:

| Function                      | Amount      |
| ----------------------------- | ----------- |
| Social Security               | \$1,461     |
| Health                        | \$912       |
| Net Interest                  | \$882       |
| Medicare                      | \$874       |
| National Defense              | \$874       |
| Income Security               | \$671       |
| Veterans' Benefits & Services | \$325       |
| Education                     | \$305       |
| Transportation                | \$137       |
| Other                         | \$311       |
| **Total Outlays**             | **\$6,752** |

In addition to the efforts of DOGE to cut outlays, the US Congress, of which both Houses are under Republican control at the time of this question, is working on the next budget under Senate reconciliation rules. Please see the [2025 Reconciliation Tracker](https://www.crfb.org/blogs/2025-reconciliation-tracker) by the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget. See also from the Wharton School of Business at the University of Pennsylvania: [The FY2025 House Budget reconciliation and Trump Administration Tax Proposals: Budgetary, Economic, and Distributional Effects](https://budgetmodel.wharton.upenn.edu/issues/2025/2/27/fy2025-house-budget-reconciliation-and-trump-tax-proposals-effects)

multiple_choice.title: Who will be the 2028 Democratic nominee for President of the United States?
multiple_choice.resolution_criteria: This question will resolve as **Yes** for the person who is selected by the Democratic Party as the Democratic nominee for President of the United States for the [2028 United States presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2028_United_States_presidential_election). If someone other than a named individual is selected this question will resolve as **Other**.
multiple_choice.description:
[Presidential elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2028_United_States_presidential_election?useskin=vector) are scheduled to be held in the United States on November 7, 2028, to elect a president and vice president for a term of four years. After winning a non-consecutive second term in the [2024 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_States_presidential_election?useskin=vector), incumbent Republican Donald J. Trump, who was the nominee of the Republican Party in three consecutive elections, is prohibited by the [22nd Amendment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twenty-second_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution?useskin=vector) from being elected to a third term as president.

Incumbent President Joe Biden won the [2024 Democratic Party presidential primary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Democratic_Party_presidential_primaries), but subsequently [withdrew his candidacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Withdrawal_of_Joe_Biden_from_the_2024_United_States_presidential_election) in July 2024, prior to the formal selection of the Democratic Party nominee. The withdrawal followed a June 27, 2024, debate with Donald Trump which raised questions about Biden's age and ability to serve a second term. Vice President [Kamala Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamala_Harris) received the Democratic Party's presidential nomination.

multiple_choice.title: Which party will hold the most seats in the US Senate after the 2026 midterm elections?
multiple_choice.resolution_criteria:
This question will resolve as the party that holds more US Senate seats than any other party in the 120th Congress, which is the one scheduled to be elected November 3, 2026 and take office in January 3, 2027.

Independent senators will be counted as part of the party they caucus with.

This question will resolve as **Other** if:

* A third party holds more seats than both Republicans and Democrats.
* Independents that do not caucus with either party hold more seats than both Republicans and Democrats.
* More seats are vacant than the ones held by both Republicans and Democrats.

If Republicans and Democrats hold an equal number of seats in the Senate and this question does not resolve as **Other**, it will resolve as **Republicans**, as the Vice President can cast the tie-breaking vote.
multiple_choice.fine_print:
Metaculus will resolve this quesiton based on the final result of the elections, incuding special elections, recounts, or run-offs.

If Democrats or Republicans change name, the options will be renamed accordingly.
multiple_choice.description:
The 2026 midterm elections are scheduled for Tuesday, November 3. The US Senate has 100 seats. [As of early 2025](https://ballotpedia.org/119th_United_States_Congress), 53 are held by members of the Republican Party, 45 are held by Democrats, and 2 are held by independents who [caucus with](https://www.senate.gov/about/glossary.htm#C) the Democrats.

Senators are elected for 6-year terms, and elections are held every two years, so in each election approximately 1/3 of the seats are up for contest. For 2026, [the 33 seats of "Class II" are scheduled for election](https://www.senate.gov/senators/Class_II.htm). As of early 2025, 20 are held by Republicans and 13 of those seats are held by Democrats. The 33 winners of the 2026 Senate elections will join 66 incumbent Senators and the winners of the concurrent House elections to form the 120th Congress.

multiple_choice.title: Which party will hold the most seats in the US House of Representatives after the 2026 elections?
multiple_choice.resolution_criteria:
This question will resolve as the party that holds more House of Representatives seats than any other party in the 120th Congress, which is the one scheduled to be elected November 3, 2026 and take office in January 3, 2027.

Independent representatives will be counted as part of the party they caucus with.

This question will resolve as **Other** if:

* Republicans and Democrats hold an equal number of seats.
* A third party holds more seats than both Republicans and Democrats.
* Independents that do not caucus with either party hold more seats than both Republicans and Democrats.
* More seats are vacant than the ones held by both Republicans and Democrats.
multiple_choice.fine_print:
Metaculus will resolve this question based on the final result of the elections, including special elections, recounts, or run-offs.

If Democrats or Republicans change name, the options will be renamed accordingly.
multiple_choice.description:
The 2026 midterm elections are scheduled for Tuesday, November 3. The US House of Representatives has 435 seats. [As of early 2025](https://ballotpedia.org/119th_United_States_Congress), 218 are held by members of the Republican Party, 215 are held by Democrats, and 2 are vacant.

Representatives are elected for 2-year terms, and elections are held every two years; so all of the seats are up for contest in every election. The winners of the 2026 House elections will join the Senate to form the 120th Congress.

multiple_choice.title: Who will be the 2028 Republican nominee for President of the United States?
multiple_choice.resolution_criteria: This question will resolve as **Yes** for the person who is selected by the Republican Party as the Republican nominee for President of the United States for the [2028 United States presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2028_United_States_presidential_election). If someone other than a named individual is selected this question will resolve as **Other**.
multiple_choice.description: [Presidential elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2028_United_States_presidential_election?useskin=vector) are scheduled to be held in the United States on November 7, 2028, to elect a president and vice president for a term of four years. After winning a non-consecutive second term in the [2024 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_States_presidential_election?useskin=vector), incumbent Republican Donald J. Trump, who was the nominee of the Republican Party in three consecutive elections, is prohibited by the [22nd Amendment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twenty-second_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution?useskin=vector) from being elected to a third term as president.

multiple_choice.title: How many times will President Donald Trump be impeached by the end of his second term?
multiple_choice.resolution_criteria: This question will resolve as the total number of times that Donald Trump is impeached as President of the United States before the conclusion of his second term in office, at noon Eastern Time on January 20, 2029.
multiple_choice.fine_print: This question will resolve as the number of times that the House of Representatives adopts any number of articles of impeachment against President Trump. The number of articles of impeachment or whether Trump is convicted by the Senate or removed from office are irrelevant. The two impeachments from the first term count, so the minimum number of impeachments is two.
multiple_choice.description:
Under the [United States Constitution](https://constitution.congress.gov/constitution/), impeachment of federal government officers, including the President, is entrusted to the House of Representatives. Impeachment is the [bringing of misconduct charges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_impeachment_in_the_United_States); once impeached, the officer may then tried on those charges by the Senate and, if convicted by the Senate, may be removed from office.

There have been [twenty-two impeachments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_impeachment_in_the_United_States#List_of_federal_impeachments) in the history of the United States, most of which were against federal judges. U.S. Presidents have been impeached only four times, and none of them were convicted by the Senate: President Andrew Johnson was impeached in 1868, President Bill Clinton was impeached in 1998, and President Donald Trump was impeached in 2019 and then again in 2021.

Trump's [2019 impeachment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_impeachment_of_Donald_Trump) centered on the accusation that he solicited foreign interference (from Ukraine) for the then-upcoming (2020) presidential election, and Trump's [2021 impeachment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_impeachment_of_Donald_Trump) centered on the accusation that he had incited the [January 6, 2021](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/January_6_United_States_Capitol_attack) attack on the U.S. Capitol, following his loss in the 2020 election. Impeachment by the House requires only a simple majority vote, and following the 2018 and 2020 elections, Democrats held a majority in the House of Representatives, allowing Trump to be impeached on largely party-line votes.

President Trump returned to office in 2025, with Republicans holding a narrow majority in the House of Representatives. Since he returned to office, articles of impeachment have been introduced twice: First, on April 28, 2025, four Democratic members of Congress brought [an assortment of claims](https://www.congress.gov/119/bills/hres353/BILLS-119hres353ih.pdf), including that Trump was obstructing justice, usurping Congress's power of appropriations, abusing his trade powers, and unconstitutionally retaliating against his perceived enemies. Second, on May 15, 2025, Rep. Al Green introduced [a resolution](https://www.congress.gov/119/bills/hres415/BILLS-119hres415ih.pdf) arguing that Trump's "authoritarian" behavior was a threat to democracy. Neither resolution was taken up by the Republican-led House.

Control of the House for the second-half of Trump's current presidential term will be decided in November 2026. As of mid-February 2026, Democrats [are favored 80/20](https://www.metaculus.com/questions/36369/us-house-plurality-after-2026-midterms/) to take back control of the House.

discrete.title: How many new national emergencies will Donald J. Trump declare under the National Emergencies Act in 2026?
discrete.fine_print:
If there is any discrepancy or ambiguity in the US Federal Register, the number most consistently reported across the US Federal Register, White House official statements and Congressional Research Service reports will be used to resolve this question.

Only declarations made while Donald J. Trump is US President will count. Any declarations made during any period(s) in 2026 he ceases to be US President will not count.
discrete.description:
The [US National Emergencies Act](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R46379#_Toc45719709) gives the US President authority to declare national emergencies, thereby unlocking a range of statutory powers. Presidents have historically declared emergencies for a wide range of issues - from foreign policy and sanctions to domestic crises. Different administrations have applied the Act in various ways and often for significantly different policy priorities.

National emergencies have been listed by [the Brennan Center for Justice](https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/declared-national-emergencies-under-national-emergencies-act).

discrete.title: How many U.S. metro areas with more than 500k people will have non-routine military or federalized National Guard deployments before Nov 3, 2026?
discrete.resolution_criteria:
This question will resolve as the total number of U.S. metropolitan statistical areas (MSAs) with a total population of more than 500,000 in which active-duty U.S. military forces or federalized National Guard units have been deployed for a non-routine domestic mission at any time after June 1, 2025 and before November 3, 2026, according to [credible sources](https://www.metaculus.com/faq/#definitions).

To count, a deployment must fulfill all of the following criteria:

1. It must consist of active duty-troops or National Guard troops called into federal service.
2. The deployed troops must be at least 30 and they must operate inside the MSA for at least 12 continuous hours.
3. The primary purpose of the deployment must be domestic, operational, and non-routine (e.g., riot control, large-scale civil disturbance, enforcing federal directives).
discrete.fine_print:
* The population threshold will be determined using the most recent U.S. Census Bureau estimate. A list of MSAs and their populations can be found [<u>here</u>](https://www.census.gov/data/tables/time-series/demo/popest/2020s-total-metro-and-micro-statistical-areas.html).
* Missions such as disaster relief, routine border operations within 100 miles of a land border, pre-planned ceremonial or training activities, and regularly scheduled National Special Security Events (e.g., the Presidential Inauguration) do not count.
* If a stated purpose for a deployment mixes an a non-routine with a routine mission, it will count.
* This question will resolve as the total number of MSAs that have at least one qualifying event take place during the period in question. In other words, an MSA will only count once, even if multiple qualifying deployments occur within its limits.
* A deployment will count if any part occurs in the period in question, meaning that the summer 2025 deployment in LA counts for the purposes of this question.
discrete.description:
Domestic deployment of federal troops to major U.S. metropolitan areas is rare and generally requires the president to invoke the Insurrection Act or otherwise place National Guard troops in Title 10 (federal) status. The most recent high-profile instance came during President Trump’s first term in response to the George Floyd protests, when about [<u>1,600 active-duty soldiers were moved into the Washington-Arlington-Alexandria MSA on 1-5 June, 2020</u>](https://thehill.com/policy/defense/500840-pentagon-moves-active-duty-units-near-dc-as-protests-escalate/). Before that, the [<u>1992 Los Angeles riots saw roughly 3,000-4,000 Army and Marine personnel deployed alongside 6,000 California National Guard troops</u>](https://www.britannica.com/event/Los-Angeles-Riots-of-1992) in the Los Angeles-Long Beach-Anaheim MSA.

Now, in his second term, a qualifying deployment has already occurred. Beginning June 9, 2025, President Trump federalized roughly [<u>4,100 California National Guard members and dispatched about 700 active-duty Marines</u>](https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2025/06/20/trump-keep-national-guard-la-ruling/) to downtown Los Angeles to protect federal facilities amid large-scale unrest during immigration protests. This recent deployment to the Los Angeles-Long Beach-Anaheim MSA meets all three criteria in the question — federal personnel, the continuous presence of more than thirty troops, and a non-routine domestic mission mission, contributing one to the eventual count.

After ordering federalized Guard troops and Marines into Los Angeles, President Trump told reporters the move was [<u>“the first, perhaps, of many” and warned that protests elsewhere “will be met with equal or greater force.”</u>](https://time.com/7294100/trump-national-guard-immigration-protests/) So far, however, no additional deployments have been announced or confirmed.

discrete.title: How many members of the Trump cabinet will remain in their positions continuously until January 20, 2029?
discrete.resolution_criteria: This question will resolve as the total number of the 15 cabinet members named in the fine print that continuously serve from June 1, 2025, to the end of Trump's term on January 20, 2029.
discrete.fine_print:
* Continuously serving includes cases where a cabinet member takes temporary leave, such as for medical reasons, including situations where a temporary acting replacement is appointed. In the event of an indefinite leave, the cabinet member will count as continuously serving so long as a replacement (excluding temporary acting replacements) has not been either nominated or appointed. Metaculus will make a judgment regarding the question resolution in the event there are unclear cases.
* The 15 cabinet members of the Second Trump Administration considered for the purposes of this question:

|  #  | Cabinet Position                           | Incumbent             |
| :-: | ------------------------------------------ | :-------------------- |
|  1  | Secretary of State                         | Marco Rubio           |
|  2  | Secretary of the Treasury                  | Scott Bessent         |
|  3  | Secretary of Defense                       | Pete Hegseth          |
|  4  | Attorney General                           | Pam Bondi             |
|  5  | Secretary of the Interior                  | Doug Burgum           |
|  6  | Secretary of Agriculture                   | Brooke Rollins        |
|  7  | Secretary of Commerce                      | Howard Lutnick        |
|  8  | Secretary of Labor                         | Lori Chavez-DeRemer   |
|  9  | Secretary of Health and Human Resources    | Robert F. Kennedy Jr. |
|  10 | Secretary of Housing and Urban Development | Scott Turner          |
|  11 | Secretary of Education                     | Linda McMahon         |
|  12 | Secretary of Veterans Affairs              | Doug Collins          |
|  13 | Secretary of Homeland Security             | Kirsti Noem           |
|  14 | Secretary of Energy                        | Chris Wright          |
|  15 | Secretary of Transportation                | Sean Duffy            |
discrete.description:
The first Trump administration was notable in having a [high turnover](https://www.bloomberg.com/graphics/2018-white-house-staffing/). Firings, resignations and dismissals across the 15 'main' cabinet positions *(see the resolution criteria fine print for the current cabinet)* far exceeded that of his predecessors like George W. Bush and Barak Obama.

![](https://cdn.metaculus.com/user_uploaded/image_iHYpXtQ.png)

[*Brookings*](https://www.brookings.edu/articles/tracking-turnover-in-the-trump-administration/)*: Cabinet Turnover By President, Through The End of Trump's First Term*

Given than cabinet members serve at the pleasure of the President, it is not entirely unusual for cabinet members to resign or be removed from their positions (two years tends to be the average), however, an emerging trend for Trump's first cabinet was that members quit fast and quit early; and recent events in the White House suggest that the trend may continue during Trump's second administration.

Perhaps the most notable piece of evidence suggesting another fractious cabinet was the [Signalgate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_government_group_chat_leaks#) scandal involving top White House personnel, three cabinet secretaries — [Marco Rubio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Rubio), Pete Hegseth and Scott Bessent — and the US Vice President, [JD Vance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JD_Vance). All three cabinet members survived, and whilst Trump's team received a bipartisan scalding, Trump appeared to remain indifferent.

Other considerations, aside from Trump's well-known volatility, are controversial appointments such as [Robert F. Kennedy Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_F._Kennedy_Jr.) as Secretary of Health and Human Resources, despite being a well-known vaccine skeptic, and [Pete Hegseth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Hegseth) as Secretary of Defense, despite a lack of experience relative to his predecessors and allegations of sexual assault on his record. Additionally, Trump's appointment of Elon Musk as a special presidential advisor and placing him in change of his cost-cutting initiative — The Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) — appeared to caused [significant tension between cabinet members](https://www.axios.com/2025/04/23/musk-bessent-trump-white-house-irs).
